title: UOps, rewrites, bounds
why: Every later week is a rewrite on one hash-consed graph of (op, src, arg) nodes. This module builds that graph, its cached dtype/shape/bounds/cost properties, and the rewrite engine you will reuse through Module 31.

steps.title: Handout page 1: the format and grammar
steps.detail: Page 1 only: the token table (DEF, REF, INT, BOOL, OP, ATTR, brackets, EOF), the 4-line grammar, the filename-prefix table and the immediate limits (bytes > 4096; nodes >= 100 or edges >= 300; cost >= 1,000,000). Write the grammar down before coding.

steps.title: Tokenizer and parser
steps.detail: Turn a .uir file into a list of bindings (name, op, atoms, attrs); handle comments, hex, leading zeros, %x= vs %x =, and [ ] sugar. Make comments_and_spacing, xor_hex, leading_zeros, stack_sugar_same parse; REJECT rejected_undefined_ref, rejected_redefined, rejected_unknown_op, rejected_int_literal_range.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: UOp is a singleton
steps.detail: UOpMetaClass keeps a cache keyed by (op, dtype, src, arg), so building the same triple twice returns the same object. Then read UOpMetaClass at the pinned commit: https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L181. The note is from Jan 2025 and the code has moved since, so trust the source.

steps.title: Interned UOp(op, src, arg)
steps.detail: Build nodes through one constructor keyed by (op, src, arg) so equal triples return the same object. hashcons_same_node.uir gives 36 either way, so also assert in a unit test that %a is %b for that file. Count distinct nodes and source edges here; overbudget_many_nodes needs the count.

steps.title: Lazy dtype and shape + validator
steps.detail: Cache dtype/shape per node and reject: rejected_add_dtype_mismatch, alu_on_vector, stack_mixed, where_cond_int, div_bool, free_param, no_assert, assert_used, assert_dtype_mismatch, unreachable, vector_return, two_params_one_slot, missing_arg, arg_dtype (all with the rejected_ prefix).

steps.title: Handout page 2: the operation reference table
steps.detail: Read the Bounds and Cost columns row by row: overflowing i32 bounds widen to I; div uses endpoint quotients only for a fixed y; mod has three cases (variable y, zero, fixed nonzero y); xor is exact only for two singletons; shl is a hull over possible k; then the two worked boxes (index safety, shared vs distinct cost).

steps.title: tinygrad UOp._min_max (vmin/vmax)
steps.detail: Read _min_max after drafting your own and note how each op derives bounds from source bounds. Then skim the tests in https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/test/null/test_uop_vmin_vmax.py.

steps.title: Bounds and index/limit safety
steps.detail: Interval bounds per the page 2 table, used to prove index and call-argument safety across all calls. Pass index_param_safe, index_mod_bounds_safe, index_stack, and REJECT rejected_index_oob, rejected_index_const_oob, rejected_index_unbounded, rejected_arg_outside_limits, rejected_limits_reversed.

steps.title: Cost and budgets
steps.detail: Charge each node once (a call costs 1 + C(body) each time it appears). Check budgets in the handout's order: bytes before parsing, nodes/edges right after parsing, cost after validation. Pass overbudget_file_size, overbudget_many_nodes, overbudget_static_cost, cost_under_budget.

steps.title: Evaluator
steps.detail: Interpret the graph with i32 wrap, floor div/mod (div by 0 gives -1, mod by 0 gives x), shl by y mod 32, bool add as OR and mul as AND, and call/param substitution. Pass every MATCH and mismatch_ file in python3 run_tests.py 1.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: Pattern matcher, then UPat/PatternMatcher source
steps.detail: Read the note (written against an older tinygrad), then the pinned source: UPat (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1429), PatternMatcher (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1572) and graph_rewrite (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1877).

steps.title: UPat + PatternMatcher + graph_rewrite to fixed point
steps.detail: A matcher over (op, src patterns, named captures) and a bottom-up rewrite loop that stops when nothing changes. Port 5 cases from https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/test/null/test_pattern_matcher.py as your own unit tests.

steps.title: Constant folding and identities
steps.detail: Rules: fold all-constant ALU through your evaluator, x+0, x*1, x*0, x^x, max(x,x), where(true,a,b). Every MATCH test must fold to assert c c. Compare with symbolic_simple: https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/symbolic.py#L123.

steps.title: Write 10 tests of your own
steps.detail: Cases an obvious-but-wrong compiler gets wrong: add at INT_MIN/INT_MAX, div/mod by a negative divisor, an index that is only out of range on the second call, shared vs distinct cost. Work out each expected result by hand from the page 2 table.

build: ./compile parses, validates, bounds-checks, costs, evaluates and constant-folds Week 1 UIR files.
check: python3 run_tests.py 1 prints 65/65 passed
A unit test shows the two add 2 4 nodes in hashcons_same_node.uir are the same object
Every MATCH test rewrites to assert c c through your PatternMatcher
10+ own tests in tests/week01 with hand-derived expected outcomes

extra.title: tinygrad-notes: Understanding the VIZ=1 tool
extra.note: Then write a Graphviz dump of your graph before and after each rewrite pass.

extra.title: tinygrad test_uop_symbolic.py
extra.note: Many symbolic identities as tests; port a few to UIR.

extra.title: tinygrad symbolic.py: symbolic
extra.note: The full simplifier you will grow toward in Module 22.

extra.title: 10-411 technical syllabus
extra.note: Week 1 section: lecture topics (bottom-up greedy rewrite engines, const folding, symbolic simplification, computer algebra systems).

outcomes: Parse UIR into an interned UOp DAG where equal (op, src, arg) triples are one object.
Compute dtype, shape, interval bounds and cost per node, and use bounds to accept or reject every index and call.
Write UPat rules and run graph_rewrite to a fixed point to fold every Week 1 MATCH test to assert c c.
stuck: Rewrites never terminate: two rules undo each other (a+b -> b+a). Canonicalize operand order once instead of swapping.
div/mod with negatives disagree: the spec is floor division (Python //), not C truncation. Test div_floor_negative and mod_negative_divisor first.
Folding changes results: you folded with Python ints. Wrap to 32 bits after every folded add, mul and shl.
Validator passes but evaluator crashes: check src count and dtype per op in the validator, not only the op name.
A rewritten child does not show up in the parent: rebuild the parent through the interning constructor when any source changes.

project.title: z3-checked symbolic simplifier with a rewrite tracer
project.brief: Turn your rewrite engine into a checked simplifier. Encode each integer rule as a z3 query over 32-bit bitvectors (wraparound included) and refuse to load any rule that z3 cannot prove under its stated preconditions. Add a tracer that records each rule firing and renders before/after graphs.
deliverables: repo with a rule file, a check_rules CLI that runs z3 on every rule, and CI that fails on an unproven rule
a Graphviz or HTML trace of each rewrite step on 3 index expressions taken from your Week 5 (Module 22) output
README table: rule count, proven/rejected, and node-count reduction on 200+ expressions (the week01-05 tests plus cases ported from tinygrad's test_uop_symbolic.py)
a 600-1200 word write-up on one rule z3 rejected, its counterexample, and the corrected precondition

rubric.solid: 30+ rules, all z3-proven at 32-bit width; measured node-count reduction on the 200+ expression set; trace works on any UIR file.
rubric.exceptional: Uses interval bounds as z3 assumptions so conditional rules (e.g. x%n -> x when 0<=x<n) are proven too; documents at least one unsound rule you wrote first, with its counterexample.

references.title: Z3 theorem prover (Python bindings via z3-solver)
egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation (POPL 2021)
Graphviz

title: Loads, stores, memory; render C
why: Memory adds effects, so graph order stops being free: a load must come after the stores it observes. This is also your first backend: toposort, emit C, compile with clang, call through ctypes.

steps.title: 10-411 syllabus: Week 2
steps.detail: Read the Week 2 section (BUFFER/ALLOC/SHRINK/LOAD/STORE/AFTER; 'Loads and stores must be fully ordered for programs to be valid') next to the README Week 2 spec, which names the buffer op extern.

steps.title: Parse nested (op ...) expressions and new ops
steps.detail: Extend the parser for extern, store, load, after, index-on-buffer, and nested parenthesised operands anywhere an atom goes. Week 1 tests must still pass.

steps.title: Russ Cox, Hardware Memory Models: 'Sequential Consistency' and 'x86 Total Store Order (x86-TSO)'
steps.detail: Only these two sections. They show why unordered memory operations can be observed out of order, which is what AFTER rules out.

steps.title: Preshing, Memory Ordering at Compile Time
steps.detail: Short post: the compiler reorders loads and stores at -O2, and a compiler barrier stops it.

steps.title: Ordering validator
steps.detail: Track, per buffer, the stores reachable through after. REJECT unordered loads and out-of-range or wrong-dtype stores, reusing Week 1 bounds. Pass rejected_load_without_after, rejected_store_oob, rejected_store_dtype.

steps.title: Interpreter support for memory
steps.detail: Extend the Week 1 evaluator with buffers so it executes store/load/after in dependency order. Pass store_load, index_store, two_stores_ordered, read_modify_write, mismatch_stale_read.

steps.title: tinygrad linearize (toposort to a list)
steps.detail: Read linearize() and UOp.toposort (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L281) to see a graph turned into a straight-line list.

steps.title: Toposort + C emitter
steps.detail: Emit one loopless C function: one local per node in topo order, buffers as pointer arguments, i32 add/mul/shl done in uint32_t and cast back so signed overflow is not undefined behaviour.

steps.title: tinygrad renderer/cstyle.py: base_rewrite and ClangRenderer
steps.detail: Read base_rewrite (lines 9-80) and ClangRenderer (line 283). Rendering is another PatternMatcher, from UOp to string.

steps.title: Python ctypes: loading shared libraries and arrays
steps.detail: Tutorial sections 'Loading dynamic link libraries', 'Specifying the required argument types (function prototypes)' and 'Arrays'. Use dlopen if your compiler is not in Python.

steps.title: clang -O2 -shared + ctypes runtime
steps.detail: Write the .c file to a temp dir, compile with clang -O2 -shared, load it, allocate buffers, call, compare with the assert. Run week01 and week02 through the C backend.

steps.title: Cross-check the two backends
steps.detail: Run the interpreter and the C backend on every test and diff the results. Add 10 tests, e.g. two stores to the same index, a store whose index is only safe via mod bounds, an add that overflows INT_MAX.

build: A C backend: toposort, render one loopless function, compile with clang, run via ctypes, with the interpreter as a cross-check.
check: python3 run_tests.py 1 and python3 run_tests.py 2 both pass with the C backend
rejected_load_without_after, rejected_store_oob and rejected_store_dtype print REJECTED
Interpreter and C backend give the same value on every test file
10+ new tests in tests/week02

extra.title: Russ Cox, Programming Language Memory Models
extra.note: Follow-up on how languages expose ordering.

extra.title: John Regehr, A Guide to Undefined Behavior in C and C++, Part 1
extra.note: Why generated signed i32 arithmetic needs the uint32_t round-trip.

outcomes: Reject a UIR program whose loads are not ordered after the stores to the same buffer.
Toposort a UOp graph, emit one loopless C function, build it with clang -O2 -shared and call it through ctypes.
Use the Week 1 interpreter as a reference to diff against the C backend on every test.
stuck: ctypes segfault: argtypes not set, or a buffer object freed before the call. Set argtypes and keep a Python reference to every buffer.
Node rendered twice or used before defined: the toposort visits shared children more than once. Memoize by node identity.
Old code runs after you change the compiler: dlopen returned the library already loaded from that path. Name each .so by a hash of its source.
C and interpreter disagree only on overflow tests: clang assumed signed add cannot overflow. Do i32 arithmetic in uint32_t.

project.title: Differential fuzzer: C backend vs interpreter
project.brief: Write a random UIR program generator for the Week 1-2 op set (i32/bool, scalars and stacks, stores and loads with after, edge-case constants like INT_MIN and 0) and differential-test your C backend against your interpreter. Shrink every mismatch to a minimal reproducer and commit it as a regression test.
deliverables: repo with a generator, a runner that compares both backends, and a delta-debugging reducer
README with programs per second, per-op coverage counts, and a table of bugs found (root cause, fix commit)
a regression corpus of minimized failing programs wired into run_tests.py-style tests
a 600-1200 word write-up on the most surprising bug and the C rule behind it

rubric.solid: 100,000+ generated programs (batch many functions per .c file to keep clang time down) with no unexplained mismatch; every mismatch found is minimized below 15 nodes and fixed.
rubric.exceptional: Generator is driven by Hypothesis strategies so shrinking is automatic; you compare its shrunk cases against your own reducer; generated programs hit every op and every REJECTED rule at least 100 times.

references.title: Csmith: random program generator for differential compiler testing
Hypothesis documentation (property-based testing)

title: Loops, floats, runtime; matmul and conv
why: range and end turn straight-line code into loop nests, and placing each computation in the innermost loop it depends on is the first scheduling decision. f32 arrives, so correctness becomes a tolerance.

steps.title: 10-411 syllabus: Week 3
steps.detail: RANGE/END/RECIP, the ranges and ended_ranges properties, and the note that this is likely the first week you need a rewrite engine to order the ranges.

steps.title: range/end/recip/f32 in parser, types and bounds
steps.detail: range n has bounds [0, n-1]; recip takes f32 only; float literals contain '.'. REJECT rejected_recip_int and rejected_range_index_oob.

steps.title: Compute a ranges property per node
steps.detail: For each node, the set of open ranges it depends on: the union over its sources, minus ranges closed by end. This decides loop placement.

steps.title: Render ranges as nested for loops
steps.detail: Emit each node inside the innermost loop among its ranges; close loops at end, innermost first. Pass range_fill, range_square, nested_ranges_2x3, float_recip.

steps.title: Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic: 'Rounding Error' and 'Relative Error and Ulps'
steps.detail: Enough to justify a 1e-4 relative tolerance and to see why summation order changes a float result.

steps.title: Float comparison in assert and runtime
steps.detail: Compare f32 results with a tolerance; emit float, not double, and render recip x as 1.0f/x.

steps.title: Hand-write gemm_256.uir
steps.detail: M=N=K=256 with three ranges and an accumulator buffer. Check against NumPy (A @ B in float32) within 1e-4 with a small harness script.

steps.title: CS231n conv notes: 'Implementation as Matrix Multiplication'
steps.detail: The im2col paragraph in the Convolutional Layer section. Write the six-loop direct conv on paper first.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: The trick in convolution and arange
steps.detail: tinygrad builds conv from _pool, which is expand, permute and shrink. Preview for Module 22; the note uses an older tinygrad API.

steps.title: Hand-write conv3x3.uir
steps.detail: Direct 3x3 conv2d, 1 channel, 32x32 input, no padding (30x30 output), as nested ranges. Check against a NumPy loop or scipy.signal.correlate2d(mode='valid') within 1e-4.

steps.title: Time gemm_256 in C
steps.detail: Report GFLOP/s (2*256^3 flops / median time over 10+ runs after a warmup) for your naive loop nest. Module 24 tries to beat this number.

steps.title: 10 own tests
steps.detail: E.g. a range of size 1, an index that is safe only because of range bounds, recip of a negative, an expression that should be placed outside the inner loop.

build: Loop nests from range/end, f32 and recip, plus hand-written GEMM and conv UIR checked against NumPy.
check: python3 run_tests.py 1, 2 and 3 all pass
gemm_256.uir matches NumPy float32 matmul within 1e-4
conv3x3.uir matches a NumPy 3x3 valid correlation within 1e-4
In the generated C, a node that depends only on the outer range is emitted outside the inner loop

extra.title: tinygrad renderer/cstyle.py: RANGE rendering in base_rewrite
extra.note: Lines 15-18: RANGE becomes a for loop.

outcomes: Lower range/end into C for loops with each node in the innermost loop it depends on.
Compare f32 results within a stated tolerance and explain why accumulation order changes them.
Hand-write GEMM (256^3) and a 3x3 conv in UIR, verify them against NumPy, and report a GFLOP/s baseline.
stuck: Wrong loop nesting or off-by-one bounds: print the generated C for nested_ranges_2x3 and trace it by hand.
conv3x3 wrong only at the edges: output size for a valid 3x3 on 32x32 is 30x30. Check your index ranges against that.
gemm_256 fails the tolerance: the oracle used float64. Compute the NumPy reference in float32, or compare with a relative tolerance.
Timings vary run to run: warm up once, time 10+ runs and report the median.

project.title: Roofline benchmark harness for your compiler
project.brief: Build a harness that runs the kernels your compiler can emit now (elementwise add over 2^20 f32, gemm at 64/128/256/512, conv3x3 at 32/64/128) over a size sweep, computes arithmetic intensity (flops / bytes of buffers) from the IR, and plots each on a roofline of your machine using a measured peak FLOP/s and a STREAM-style copy bandwidth. Later modules add their kernels to it.
deliverables: repo with a bench CLI that writes JSON results keyed by git commit
a generated HTML or notebook page: roofline plot, GFLOP/s vs size, history across commits
the two microbenchmarks (peak FLOP/s, memory bandwidth) and their measured numbers
a 600-1200 word write-up on which kernels are compute- or memory-bound and why

rubric.solid: All listed kernels on one roofline with intensity computed from the IR, not hand-entered; repeated runs agree within 5%; NumPy float32 matmul shown as a reference point.
rubric.exceptional: CI flags any kernel that slows down by more than 5% between commits; adds an L1/L2 bandwidth ceiling and explains which gemm sizes fall out of cache.

title: Rangeify, reduce, materialization
why: Rangeify lowers shaped ops to scalar code over explicit ranges and decides which values get a buffer. Fuse-or-stage is the scheduling decision every ML compiler makes.

steps.title: 10-411 syllabus: Week 4
steps.detail: REDUCE (axis count / op), STAGE (temp buffer), EXPAND, and 'Rangeify removes shapes from all ops'.

steps.title: expand, reduce, rank-1 ALU: types and shapes
steps.detail: Shape rules for expand (scalar to (n,)) and reduce of the last pop axes. REJECT rejected_shape_mismatch; pass elementwise_rank1 in the interpreter first.

steps.title: Halide (PLDI 2013) sections 1-3
steps.detail: Section 3, 'Scheduling Image Processing Pipelines': 3.1 walks a two-stage blur through inline, root and tiled schedules; 3.2 models a schedule as where each stage is computed and where it is stored. Skip section 5 (autotuning).

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: Short note on operator fusion
steps.detail: a+4+3 becomes one kernel; calling realize() on the intermediate forces two. Written against an older tinygrad.

steps.title: Rangeify pass
steps.detail: Rewrite each shaped node into a scalar node indexed by ranges: elementwise ops share their consumer's ranges; reduce opens new ranges and an accumulator. Pass dot_product, reduce_max, reduce_expand, mismatch_reduce.

steps.title: tinygrad run_rangeify and pm_apply_rangeify
steps.detail: After your first version: run_rangeify, the pm_apply_rangeify matcher (line 128) and convert_reduce_to_reduce_with_ranges (line 104).

steps.title: Materialization decision
steps.detail: Fuse elementwise chains into one loop. Insert a staged temp buffer only when a value is needed under different ranges, e.g. a reduce input that is read twice.

steps.title: tinygrad rangeify.py: stage, _limit_bufs, remove_bufferize
steps.detail: stage() wraps a value in a bufferize over fresh ranges and indexes it back; _limit_bufs (line 169) calls it when a kernel would exceed the device's buffer limit. remove_bufferize (line 46) goes the other way.

steps.title: Inspect generated C for reduce(mul(a,b))
steps.detail: Expect one loop, no temp buffer, and the accumulator as a local scalar.

steps.title: Count kernels/buffers per test
steps.detail: Print loop count and temp-buffer count per test program; commit the table and fail if it changes unexpectedly.

steps.title: 10 own tests
steps.detail: E.g. x minus max(x) (the reduce input is used twice, so it must stage), expand of a reduce, max-reduce of all-negative values (init to INT_MIN, not 0).

build: A rangeify pass that lowers expand/reduce/rank-1 ALU to scalar loops and decides fusion vs staging.
check: python3 run_tests.py 1 through 4 all pass
reduce(mul(a,b)) generates one loop with no temp buffer in the C
A reduce input read twice gets exactly one staged buffer
10+ new tests in tests/week04

extra.title: Chen et al., TVM section 4 (Generating Tensor Operations)
extra.note: 4.1 covers the tensor expression and schedule space: another take on the algorithm/schedule split.

extra.title: TorchInductor design post
extra.note: See the answer on op fusion: can_fuse decides legality and score_fusion orders fusions.

outcomes: Lower expand, reduce and rank-1 ALU to scalar loops over explicit ranges.
Decide per value whether to fuse it into its consumer or stage it in a temp buffer, and show the decision in the generated C.
Count loops and temp buffers per program and keep the counts as a regression check.
stuck: A fused reduce is recomputed for every output element: stage a reduce result that is consumed inside another loop.
Wrong results after fusion: two reduces share range variables. Give each reduce its own ranges.
Accumulator carries over between outputs: initialize it inside the outer loops, not above them.
reduce_max wrong on negative inputs: the identity for max is INT_MIN (or -inf for f32), not 0.

project.title: Fusion plan search with a cost model
project.brief: Expose each fuse-or-stage decision as a knob. Enumerate the plans for three rank-1 graphs you can write in Week 4 UIR, estimate bytes moved and flops for each with a cost model, measure real runtime, and report how well the model ranks the plans.
deliverables: repo with a plan enumerator, a cost model and a runner
README with predicted vs measured time and Spearman rank correlation on 3 graphs at n = 2^20 f32: x*recip(sum(x)), x - max(x), and a mean-centered sum of squares
the generated C for the chosen plan next to the no-fusion plan, with temp-buffer sizes noted
a 600-1200 word write-up on a case where fusing made things slower and why

rubric.solid: For each graph the chosen plan is at least as fast as both no-fusion and fuse-everything; Spearman correlation of at least 0.7 between predicted and measured time across all plans.
rubric.exceptional: Cost model includes a cache-size term fitted from your Module 20 bandwidth numbers and the correlation improves measurably; one counterintuitive case explained with measured numbers.

title: Movement ops
why: reshape, permute, pad, shrink and expand never copy: each becomes index arithmetic, plus a validity mask for pad. Simplifying the resulting div/mod with bounds decides whether the generated loops are clean.

steps.title: ezyang, PyTorch internals: the 'strides' and 'views' part
steps.detail: The strides, views and storage part near the start of the essay (before the section on autograd and the codebase tour). Work its slicing example by hand.

steps.title: Tensor Puzzles: all 21
steps.detail: Each puzzle reimplements one NumPy function in one line using only broadcasting, arithmetic, comparison and indexing (no view or sum). This trains the index thinking movement ops need.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: Shapetracker
steps.detail: Shape, strides and mask per view, and the transpose-then-reshape example whose index needs %3 and //3. ShapeTracker has since been removed from tinygrad; the index ideas still apply.

steps.title: Shapes of any rank + shape rules for 5 movement ops
steps.detail: Validate each op's argument: reshape keeps the element count, permute is a permutation, pad/shrink pairs fit the axis. REJECT rejected_reshape_size.

steps.title: Movement ops as index rewrites
steps.detail: During rangeify, map output ranges to input indices: permute reorders them, shrink adds the start offset, expand drops the broadcast axis, reshape flattens and splits with div/mod, pad subtracts 'before' and adds a where on validity. Pass transpose_index, pad_zeros.

steps.title: tinygrad apply_movement_op and _apply_reshape
steps.detail: Compare with your version; _apply_reshape is at line 147.

steps.title: tinygrad divandmod.py: fold_divmod_general
steps.detail: Rules that use bounds: mod folds when x//y is constant; (x%(k*c))//c becomes (x//c)%k; exact division (q*c+k)//c becomes q+k//c.

steps.title: Bounds-driven div/mod simplification
steps.detail: Add div/mod rules that use your Week 1 bounds so reshape followed by the inverse reshape gives plain range indices. Check that the generated C for a contiguous reshape has no / or %.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: The trick in matrix multiplication
steps.detail: Matmul as add an axis, permute, expand, multiply, sum over the shared axis.

steps.title: Matmul and conv from movement ops
steps.detail: Pass matmul_2x2. Then write conv2d (1 channel, 8x8 input, 3x3 kernel, pad 1) using only pad, shrink, reshape, expand, permute, mul and reduce, and match NumPy.

steps.title: 10 own tests
steps.detail: E.g. permute then reshape (needs div/mod), pad then shrink back to the original, expand after permute, shrink to a single element.

build: Rank-N shapes and the five movement ops lowered to masked index arithmetic, with bounds-driven div/mod simplification.
check: python3 run_tests.py 1 through 5 all pass
conv2d built only from movement ops plus mul/reduce matches NumPy
A contiguous reshape and its inverse produce no / or % in the generated C
All 21 Tensor Puzzles pass their notebook tests

extra.title: tinygrad test_uop_symbolic.py div/mod tests
extra.note: Use its div/mod cases as tests for your simplifier.

extra.title: NumPy: Internal organization of NumPy arrays
extra.note: Strides and views from NumPy's side.

outcomes: Lower reshape, permute, expand, pad and shrink to index expressions with no copies.
Simplify div/mod index expressions using interval bounds until contiguous cases have none.
Build matmul and conv2d from movement ops plus mul and reduce.
stuck: permute then reshape gives wrong values: the reshape must split the flat index of the permuted shape, not the original one.
Pad then permute then shrink gives wrong edges: the validity mask is attached to the wrong axis. Test that exact chain.
Index expressions keep growing: add the rule (x//a)*a + x%a -> x and apply it with bounds.
rejected_reshape_size passes validation: compare the product of all dims, not the rank.

project.title: Property-tested view algebra with a z3-checked index simplifier
project.brief: Use Hypothesis to generate random chains of movement ops on random shapes, check your lowered index arithmetic against the same chain in NumPy, and prove each div/mod rule with z3 under the bounds you computed. Measure how much the simplifier shrinks index expressions on conv2d and matmul.
deliverables: repo with a Hypothesis suite (random chains up to depth 8, shapes up to rank 4) and a z3 proof for each index rule
README with index-expression op counts and generated-C line counts before and after simplification for conv2d (3x3, 32x32, pad 1), matmul 64x64 and 20 random chains

steps.detail: Write one sentence of the form 'X is N% faster/smaller than Y on Z', the metric, the baseline, and what is out of scope.

steps.title: Baseline
steps.detail: Get the reference (PyTorch, llm.c, cuBLAS, current compiler) running and record numbers.

steps.title: Benchmark harness
steps.detail: One script runs baseline and yours, checks outputs match, records the median of N runs plus GPU model, driver and library versions, and appends to a CSV.

steps.title: First full harness run
steps.detail: Run the harness end to end and commit the baseline numbers.

steps.title: Write a one-page proposal and get one reviewer
steps.detail: Claim, primary metric, baseline, kill criteria; post it for feedback before coding.

build: A chosen project with a written scope, a running baseline and a reproducible harness.
check: Scope document with goal, metric, baseline
Baseline runs and numbers are recorded
Harness checks correctness and timing reproducibly
outcomes: State the project as a falsifiable claim with one primary metric.
Run a benchmark harness that pins versions and records hardware.
Measure the strongest public baseline (PyTorch, cuBLAS, llm.c, tinygrad) for your target.
stuck: Scope too big: if you cannot state the result as 'X is N% faster/smaller than Y on Z', narrow it.
Weak baseline: comparing against your own unoptimized code proves nothing; use the best public implementation.
Harness not reproducible: pin versions, record GPU clocks and driver, run 3+ trials and report variance.
Picking a project nobody can evaluate: choose a number (speed, memory, bugs found), not 'clean design'.

project.title: Capstone phase 1: proposal, baseline and public harness
project.brief: Write a one-page proposal (problem, claim, primary metric, baseline, risks, stretch goal) and get feedback from at least one other person (forum, Discord, a peer). Publish the harness repo with baseline numbers before you write any optimization code.
deliverables: public repo with harness, pinned environment and baseline results
one-page proposal in the repo (claim, metric, baseline, timeline, kill criteria)
a baseline table with mean and variance over 3+ runs, plus the roofline bound for the target
written feedback from one reviewer and your response

rubric.solid: Claim is falsifiable; baseline is the strongest public implementation; anyone can reproduce baseline numbers in under 30 minutes.
rubric.exceptional: Harness runs in CI; the proposal states the roofline ceiling for the target and the expected gap before any optimization code exists.

references.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper
How to Scale Your Model: All About Rooflines

title: Final project: build and iterate
why: Implement the core idea in small measured steps, keeping a log of what did not work; negative results are part of the report.

steps.title: Core implementation, smallest version
steps.detail: Get the simplest end-to-end version through the harness, correct first.

steps.title: Profile where time goes
steps.detail: Use Nsight Compute (GPU) or perf (CPU) to find the bottleneck before each change.

steps.title: Scaling Book: roofline
steps.detail: Compute arithmetic intensity and the roofline bound for your target so you know the ceiling.

steps.title: Iterate: one change per commit
steps.detail: Each change: hypothesis, measurement, kept or reverted, logged.

steps.title: Regression suite
steps.detail: All course tests plus project correctness tests on every iteration.

steps.title: Ablations
steps.detail: Turn each optimization off individually and measure contribution.

steps.title: Keep a public lab notebook
steps.detail: Dated entries: hypothesis, profile evidence, result, keep/revert. Negative results included.

build: The core project implementation with measured iterations and ablations.
check: Core implementation runs correctly through the harness
Results vs baseline recorded
Experiment log includes failed attempts
All course tests still pass
outcomes: Attribute your result to specific changes with an on/off ablation table.
Show profiler evidence for every optimization you kept.
stuck: Optimizing without profiling: always record the profiler evidence that motivated a change.
Many changes per commit: you will not know what helped. One change, one measurement, one log line.
Ignoring negative results: log them; they are part of the report and show judgment.
Correctness drifts silently: run the full test suite on every iteration, including the interpreter cross-check from module 19.
Stuck on one bottleneck for more than two days: log what you tried, ask in GPU MODE or tinygrad Discord, or switch to the stretch goal.

project.title: Capstone phase 2: lab notebook and ablations
project.brief: Implement the core idea through the harness and keep a public lab notebook: every experiment with hypothesis, profile evidence, result and decision. Finish with a full ablation table and a mid-point update post.
deliverables: repo with tagged commits for each milestone and a LAB_NOTEBOOK.md with 15+ dated entries
ablation table: each component on/off with mean and variance
plots: metric over iterations, roofline position before and after
a 600–1200 word mid-project update (blog post or forum thread) with current numbers and open problems

rubric.solid: Beats or matches the baseline on the primary metric with ablations explaining the gain; all regression tests pass.
rubric.exceptional: Clear win over a strong public baseline, or a negative result with a root cause; at least one issue or PR filed upstream.

references.title: Nsight Compute Profiling Guide
Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks

title: Final project: results and write-up
why: Writing it up as a short paper forces you to state what you claim and back it with numbers.

steps.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper
steps.detail: Use its advice: state one key idea, list contributions explicitly, show examples before generality.

steps.title: Final benchmark run
steps.detail: Fresh run of the harness on clean hardware; tables and plots.

steps.title: Write the 4-page report
steps.detail: Problem, method, results, ablations, negative results, limitations.

steps.title: Clean up code and README
steps.detail: Reproduction instructions for the harness.

steps.title: End-to-end demo
steps.detail: README Week 6 milestones: MNIST MLP to at least 97% test accuracy, and stories15M producing the same tokens as llama2.c run.c.

steps.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Give a Great Research Talk
steps.detail: One key idea; examples before generality.

steps.title: Record a 15-minute talk with demo and publish
steps.detail: Slides, live demo, link from README; share publicly and collect feedback.

build: Code, a reproducible harness, a 4-page report and a 15-minute recorded talk with demo.
check: 4-page report with results and negative results
Harness reproduces the numbers
Compiler trains MNIST to >=97% and stories15M matches run.c tokens
15-minute talk with working demo recorded and published
outcomes: Write a 4-page report whose headline claim is backed by a reproducible number.
Package code so a stranger reproduces your results from the README.
stuck: Report lists what you did instead of what you found: lead with the claim and the headline number.
Plots without baselines or error bars: every chart needs a comparison and variance.
Talk too detailed: one idea, one key figure, one demo; backup slides for the rest.
Reproduction fails on a fresh machine: test the README on a clean container or cloud VM before publishing.

project.title: Capstone phase 3: public technical report, talk and demo
project.brief: Publish a 4-page report (PDF or blog post), a 15-minute recorded talk with a demo (MNIST training, stories15M generation, and the project result), and a reproducible repo. Post it publicly and record the feedback.
deliverables: public repo with one-command reproduction and a results table matching the report
4-page report: problem, method, results, ablations, negative results, limitations, related work
15-minute recorded talk with slides and demo, linked from the README
a short post (blog, X, HN, tinygrad/GPU MODE Discord) with the headline figure, and notes on feedback received

rubric.solid: Report is self-contained and every number reproduces; talk fits 15 minutes with a working demo.
rubric.exceptional: Someone else reproduces your headline number from the README and says so publicly, or the report is submitted to a workshop.

references.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper
Simon Peyton Jones, How to Give a Great Research Talk
